- When Firm B prices at $1.55, our profit is highest at $25.40 with our price $1.55, slightly better than $24.76 at $1.60. 
- When B is $1.50, our $1.50 price yields $23.42 profit, while $1.60 drops to $22.27. 
- When B rises to $1.65, a $1.60 price captures a demand surge, giving $29.69 profit (much higher than $23.74 at $1.65). 
- When B spikes to $1.80, a low price $1.50 yields $34.81 profit, indicating strong upside when B is high. 
- Prices above $1.70 generally reduce profit unless B is also high. 
- The most frequent B price is $1.55 (≈70% of rounds), followed by $1.45‑$1.50, with occasional $1.65 and rare $1.80.
119.plans:
1. Adopt a reactive rule: 
   • If Firm B’s price ≥ $1.65, set our price = $1.60 (just below B) to capture the surge. 
   • Otherwise (B < $1.65), set our price = $1.55 (matches the dominant B level and maximizes profit at $25.40). 
2. After each round, record B’s price, our quantity, margin, and profit. 
3. If B stays ≥ $1.65 for two consecutive rounds, test raising our price to $1.65 (but not above B‑0.05) to see if profit stays high. 
4. If B falls ≤ $1.45 for three consecutive rounds, revert to $1.50 to protect margin. 
5. Continuously update the rule thresholds based on observed profit changes, never pricing below cost ($1.00) or above $4.51. 
6. Document any deviation from the rule in INSIGHTS for the next update.
119.insights:
• Matching B at $1.55 yields the best consistent profit; being above B hurts profit, being below B only helps when B is unusually high. 
• A price of $1.60 is optimal only when B is $1.65 or higher, delivering a large profit boost. 
• The market rarely exceeds $1.80, so aggressive high pricing (> $1.70) offers no long‑term benefit. 
• Maintaining flexibility with a simple conditional rule balances upside in high‑B periods while protecting margin in the typical $1.55 regime.
